meta.title: GPT-6.1 Sol · Materials science · solo · run 1
meta.note: Main run, 60 minutes. The verifier accepted 4 of 5 credited claims; 3 set a new best held-out result on their dataset. Verdicts from the re-run of the official verifier.

artifacts.title: Preserving solute identities improves composition-only prediction of steel yield strength
artifacts.summary: A small-data steel model uses elemental atomic fractions directly rather than compressing all solutes into pooled elemental-property statistics. Predictions average ExtraTrees regressors fit to raw, square-root, and log-shifted fractions. The final configuration was checked on a fresh shuffled validation split after initial model screening. Additional repeated shuffled splits showed the same large gain. An ablation holding the ExtraTrees learner fixed also favored solute fractions over the baseline pooled descriptors. This is a predictive result, not a causal metallurgical model: processing history is unavailable, and validation/held-out claims concern alloys sampled from this dataset rather than extrapolation to new steel families. The released test retrains solely on public steel targets and emits predictions for evaluator-provided compositions.
artifacts.reason: accepted: hidden MAE: model beats the environment baseline (difference -37.8660, 95% CI [-64.2274, -14.9324], beyond the minimum effect 2.1817)

claim.statement: For this steel-alloy dataset, an ensemble of solute-identity-preserving concentration models reduces yield-strength MAE relative to the supplied pooled-composition boosting baseline.

artifacts.title: A representation ensemble improves composition-only experimental metallicity classification
artifacts.summary: The model averages two histogram-boosted tree classifiers trained on richer elemental statistics. Both retain elemental fractions; one also represents stoichiometry ordered by elemental identity and abundance. No band-gap labels or cross-dataset target lookups are used. Hyperparameters were frozen before a fresh shuffled validation split. The claim concerns predictive error on the provided distribution; it does not identify a physical mechanism and cannot resolve polymorph-dependent metallicity from composition alone.
artifacts.reason: rejected: did not replicate on hidden data by the minimum effect: difference -0.0098, 95% CI [-0.0196, 0.0008], needed below -0.0015

claim.statement: An equal-weight ensemble of rich elemental-statistics and ordered-stoichiometry classifiers reduces experimental metallicity classification error relative to the supplied baseline.

artifacts.title: Loss-aware mixture medians improve prediction of experimental band gaps with metallic zeros
artifacts.summary: Experimental band gaps mix an exact zero-gap metallic class with positive continuous gaps. Under absolute-error loss, the conditional median is zero when the probability of a positive gap is at most one half; otherwise it is the positive-gap conditional quantile 1 - 0.5 / P(gap>0). The implementation averages two positive-gap classifiers, fits a grid of positive-gap quantile regressors, sorts their outputs to remove quantile crossing, and interpolates the loss-optimal quantile. Classifiers, regressors, and all preprocessing are trained within each validation fold. No auxiliary dataset labels are used. The configuration was frozen before fresh validation. The paired ablation uses the same classifiers and positive-gap quantile fits but hard-gates the positive-gap median; the mixture median improves this comparator as well as direct regression. Composition alone cannot resolve polymorphism or measurement-condition effects; distribution shift is not claimed to be solved.
artifacts.reason: accepted: hidden MAE: model beats the environment baseline (difference -0.1312, 95% CI [-0.1640, -0.1007], beyond the minimum effect 0.0084)

claim.statement: For composition-only experimental band-gap prediction evaluated by MAE, a zero-inflated conditional mixture median outperforms both the supplied direct-regression baseline and a hard-gated positive-gap median.

artifacts.title: Leaf-distribution medians beat ordinary forest means for absolute-error band-gap prediction
artifacts.summary: This controlled comparison trains a single ExtraTrees forest on all experimental band-gap targets, including exact metallic zeros. The ordinary arm averages fitted tree means. The alternative assigns equal weight to trees, distributes each tree's weight uniformly over training samples in the query leaf, and returns the resulting conditional target-distribution median. Thus both arms share every fitted split and training label; only prediction aggregation changes. A configuration selected in exploratory validation was checked on fresh folds. This simpler approach independently supports loss-aware distributional prediction without a separate metal classifier or positive-gap quantile boosting. The claim is predictive and specific to absolute-error evaluation, not evidence of a causal materials mechanism.
artifacts.reason: accepted: hidden MAE: arm a beats the other arm (difference -0.0707, 95% CI [-0.0904, -0.0516], beyond the minimum effect 0.0079)

claim.statement: For experimental band gaps evaluated by MAE, the conditional median of forest leaf distributions outperforms the ordinary mean prediction from exactly the same fitted ExtraTrees forest.

artifacts.title: Subsampled composition-tree ensembles improve metallic-glass formation classification
artifacts.summary: The method averages subsampled boosted-tree classifiers using identity-preserving elemental fractions, richer elemental-property statistics, and ordered stoichiometry. A decision threshold was selected during exploratory validation and frozen before a fresh validation split. The final paired comparison improves on the supplied composition baseline. Earlier local-kernel, categorical-alloy-system, pair-descriptor, and capacity-only studies produced small or split-sensitive gains; those are not claimed as established improvements. This model predicts labels in the melt-spun alloy dataset, not general bulk-glass formation or processing-independent glass stability. New-alloy-system extrapolation remains a separate question.
artifacts.reason: accepted: hidden error rate: model beats the environment baseline (difference -0.0290, 95% CI [-0.0414, -0.0166], beyond the minimum effect 0.0025)

claim.statement: A frozen subsampled composition-tree ensemble reduces classification error for the provided metallic-glass dataset relative to the supplied pooled-composition baseline.

artifacts.title: Independent and grouped-validation checks for the released composition models
artifacts.summary: Additional unchanged-model checks support the main predictive results. The band-gap mixture median remains better than direct regression and hard gating when identical compositions are grouped, and when entire element combinations are grouped. Leaf-distribution forest medians also beat the same forests’ ordinary means under held-out element-system validation. The metallicity ensemble improves on another independent shuffled split. The original steel concentration ensemble retains its large baseline gain under grouped-composition validation; exploratory residual boosting improves further but the original published model is unchanged. Held-out input interfaces for steel, metallicity, band-gap mixture, and forest comparison were exercised using temporary input tables without target columns. These checks do not establish robustness to unobserved experimental conditions, processing, polymorphs, or arbitrary distribution shift. Quantities below appear in the listed recorded experiments; repeated quantity names refer to different validation schemes, in summary order.
artifacts.reason: not credited: notes are never credited

claim.statement: The released composition-model gains are not confined to the original exploratory split; independent and grouped-validation checks reproduce their principal baseline advantages.

artifacts.title: Glass ensemble replication and held-out alloy-system validation
artifacts.summary: The frozen glass ensemble was evaluated without changing its descriptors, fitted-model configuration, or decision threshold. Another shuffled validation split reproduces its baseline advantage. Grouping all compositions with the same element set into the same fold also preserves the relative advantage, although both methods have substantially higher absolute classification error. Thus the method transfers better than the comparator in this check, but new-system prediction remains appreciably harder than within-distribution interpolation. The final held-out prediction interface was also tested with target-free input tables. These checks support the published method without establishing processing-independent glass stability or bulk-glass discovery performance. Quantities below list shuffled validation first, then element-system-grouped validation.
artifacts.reason: not credited: notes are never credited

claim.statement: The frozen metallic-glass ensemble improves over the supplied baseline on another independent shuffled split and on held-out element-system validation.

events.text: I’ll inspect the experiment and publication requirements, then choose a tractable problem where a reproducible improvement is plausible.
I’ll examine the baseline models and data formats so the research targets a real weakness rather than an arbitrary benchmark.
I’ll read the baseline implementation separately and inspect representative records before designing validation experiments.
I’ll inspect feature construction and dataset overlap, then benchmark stronger composition models with leakage-aware validation.

I’ll test composition-aware kernels and richer elemental statistics against the supplied boosting baseline. I’ll also audit overlap between the electronic-property datasets before using any auxiliary labels.
The first recorded audit failed because the baseline module was not present in the execution snapshot. I’ll inspect the workspace and make the experiment self-contained.
I’ll diagnose module resolution inside the recorded environment rather than assume it matches the interactive shell.
I’ll explicitly add the experiment directory to Python’s import path, avoiding environment-specific import behavior.

The audit confirms substantial electronic-dataset overlap, so I’ll avoid treating those labels as independent validation evidence. My first benchmark uses identical folds for all models and tests elemental fractions, richer property statistics, and local composition kernels.
The initial benchmark jobs have returned. I’ll inspect their recorded metrics and prioritize models with consistent, substantial gains.

The steel result suggests that preserving individual solute identities matters more than aggregate elemental statistics. I’ll summarize all four screens and then validate the strongest candidates on additional splits.
I’ll investigate three concrete mechanisms: solute-specific effects in steels, local interpolation within alloy systems for glass formation, and separating metallic zeros from positive band gaps.
I’ll now test zero-inflated band-gap models. Validation will exclude each held-out composition from both electronic datasets, preventing auxiliary-label leakage.

Steel improvements are stable across several concentration representations, while glass kernels did not outperform boosted descriptors. I’ll strengthen glass validation and test whether band-gap regression provides useful auxiliary information for metallicity classification.

I’ll check the running studies and examine alloy-system structure. Glass-forming behavior may benefit from explicitly distinguishing element combinations rather than treating atomic numbers only as continuous variables.

I’ll test a hierarchical glass model: a transferable descriptor-based prior corrected by nearby measurements within the same alloy system. This directly targets the repeated composition series identified by the audit.
I’ll prepare a confirmatory steel study with fixed models and repeated paired splits. This will distinguish a robust representation gain from a lucky validation partition.

While confirmatory runs proceed, I’ll test smooth, solute-specific Gaussian-process models for steels. Their learned length scales can reveal whether nonlinear concentration sensitivity explains the tree-model gains.
I’ll inspect the publication schema and design the final prediction entry point now, so successful findings can be independently rerun without manual intervention.

I’ll add physically motivated electronic descriptors—pairwise ionic character, radius mismatch, valence fractions, and anion/cation summaries—and test whether they improve metallicity prediction beyond generic composition statistics.

I’ll test categorical alloy-system identifiers for glass formation. Unlike numeric atomic-number summaries, these let boosting learn system-specific behavior while retaining transferable descriptors for unseen systems.

The local glass correction looks promising. I’ll also test a band-gap model matched to absolute-error loss: predict the median of a mixture containing a metallic point mass at zero and a continuous positive-gap distribution.
I’ll review completed studies and freeze candidate configurations before confirmatory validation, rather than keep selecting against the same folds.
I’ll test explicit element-pair identities for glass formation. Pair interactions are chemically plausible and may transfer across ternary systems more effectively than a whole-system identifier.
Several complementary studies are running. I’ll allow them to finish before launching more searches, preserving compute for independent confirmation and final reproducibility checks.
I’ll review the completed evidence, focusing on gains that persist across splits and on whether more complex mechanisms actually outperform simple ensembles.
The steel representation gain survives repeated validation. I’ll package that model with a held-out prediction interface and a paired baseline check, then publish it before pursuing weaker effects.
I’ll check long-running studies for completion and record the steel release result. If the final implementation reproduces the gain, I can publish a precise, limited claim.

I’ll quantify how much genuinely additional information the metallicity dataset offers for band-gap learning. Any inferred zero-gap examples must be experimentally labeled metallic and excluded by composition during validation.
I’ll inspect completed final-model and mechanism tests. The auxiliary-label audit shows little new zero-gap supervision, so I’ll prioritize models trained directly on their own targets.
The released steel implementation reproduces the improvement on a new split. I’ll publish the result with explicit validation limits and a held-out prediction test.
I’ll freeze the promising glass model and evaluate it on new folds. Its local correction uses cross-fitted residuals within identical element sets, so it cannot simply memorize training-label errors.

The metallicity screen favors a simple ensemble of descriptor models, not inferred band-gap thresholds. I’ll validate that frozen ensemble separately and retain auxiliary-gap results only as exploratory evidence.
I’ll inspect the remaining studies and check for timeouts. The next decisions will use completed recorded experiments rather than partial output.

Metallicity improvements hold on the fresh validation split, while the glass gain is smaller and uncertain. I’ll publish the former with a restrained claim and keep investigating glass rather than overstate its current evidence.

I’ll validate a conservative band-gap ensemble now: a flexible tree regressor plus absolute-loss boosting, with small predicted gaps clipped to zero. This avoids depending on the more elaborate mixture-model search.
I’ll check whether the larger searches have completed and verify the prediction-interface smoke tests. Any timed-out search will be treated as exploratory only.

The mixture-median band-gap model substantially outperforms the simple ensemble in exploratory validation. I’ll implement it as a frozen candidate and compare it with both direct regression and a hard-gated positive-gap model on fresh folds.

I’ll check whether richer glass representations improve enough to warrant a new confirmatory model. I’ll also inspect the zero-inflation ablations to see whether the band-gap benefit comes from separating zeros or from choosing the correct conditional quantile.
I’ll run a focused glass comparison using larger, more local trees and the two descriptor representations. The earlier screen suggests tree capacity matters more than smooth composition kernels.
I’ll inspect the richer-feature studies and smoke tests, then decide which models deserve publication rather than extending the search indiscriminately.

I’ll test whether steel trees leave systematic nonlinear bias that can be corrected without sacrificing robustness. This is a secondary investigation; the already-published concentration model remains unchanged.

I’ll review the focused comparisons. The key band-gap question is whether the mixture median beats hard gating, which would support a loss-aware modeling contribution rather than just a larger ensemble.

I’ll test a small, complementary glass ensemble using randomized forests and histogram boosting. These learners have different biases from LightGBM and may improve prediction without adding speculative physical descriptors.
I’ll review the latest completed validation and then run a second independent band-gap confirmation if the mixture model remains clearly better.
The mixture median improves both baseline regression and hard gating on fresh folds. I’ll publish that loss-aware result and run a second confirmation that groups duplicate compositions together.
I’ll verify the band-gap result under grouped-composition validation and inspect the completed glass capacity study before choosing its final model.

I’ll analyze glass errors by alloy-system support and assess whether local corrections help only well-sampled systems. That will clarify the method’s limitations even if its overall gain remains modest.
The error audit used a literal input path that does not match this execution environment. I’ll use the provided input-directory variable and rerun it.

The glass error audit suggests local correction helps mainly in well-sampled systems. I’ll test bagging and decision thresholds next, while checking whether the band-gap mixture generalizes across entirely held-out element combinations.

I’ll test a nonparametric counterpart to the mixture model: conditional quantiles from forest-leaf target distributions. This checks whether the improvement is specific to quantile boosting or reflects the broader benefit of distribution-aware prediction.
I’ll review completed confirmation runs and stop any line of investigation that fails to improve on the simpler published methods.
The metallicity gain persists on another independent split. I’ll now test whether the small steel residual-boosting gain also survives fresh validation, without changing the published model.
I’ll check the remaining studies and use their results to choose whether glass warrants a contribution. I’ll avoid publishing a marginal improvement unless a fresh paired evaluation supports it.
I’ll review grouped validation and the forest-quantile comparison. These are robustness checks on the main band-gap finding, not opportunities to tune against the confirmation folds.

The steel residual-boosting improvement survives several fresh splits, and grouped-composition validation supports the band-gap result. I’ll now run one focused glass confirmation comparing a fixed capacity ensemble with and without the local correction.
I’ll inspect the final robustness studies. These results will determine whether to revise the steel release, publish glass, or leave those methods at their current scope.

The band-gap advantage persists when entire element combinations are held out. Glass improvements remain small with uncertainty spanning no gain, so I won’t publish them as established. I’ll make one final paired check before updating the steel method.
I’ll review the final steel check and the remaining glass studies. If none shows a reliable gain, I’ll use the remaining time to document robustness rather than add unsupported claims.

The steel residual model improves consistently but only modestly over the original. I’ll preserve the published model for now and examine whether forest quantiles or glass bagging provide a clearer additional result.

I’ll inspect the released feature definitions and remaining jobs for reproducibility risks. The final record should distinguish robust findings from exploratory improvements that did not justify publication.
I’ll let the last glass and distributional-forest studies finish, then compare their predictions directly with the frozen candidates. No further broad hyperparameter search is needed.
I’ll review the final studies and prepare a consolidated reproducibility record. The strongest results so far are the steel representation gain, metallicity ensemble, and loss-aware band-gap model.

Forest-leaf medians also look promising for band gaps, suggesting that matching the estimator to absolute-error loss matters beyond boosting. I’ll confirm that mechanism on fresh folds and separately validate the calibrated glass ensemble.
I’ll document the distinction between predictive findings and mechanisms, and run one more grouped steel check to ensure duplicate compositions are not driving its large baseline gain.

I’ll inspect the last confirmatory runs. The forest comparison isolates median-versus-mean aggregation using identical fitted trees, making it a cleaner mechanism test than comparing unrelated regressors.
The forest median beats the mean of the same fitted trees on fresh validation, supporting a distinct loss-alignment finding. I’ll publish that controlled comparison and verify its held-out interface.
I’ll inspect the calibrated glass confirmation and final interface checks. I’ll publish glass only if this frozen model produces a meaningful fresh-split gain.
I’ll review the final glass confirmation and forest robustness check. Any remaining contribution should add a distinct, reproducible result rather than duplicate the existing band-gap claims.
The frozen glass ensemble now shows a meaningful gain on fresh validation. I’ll publish it with its split-sensitivity caveat and run another unchanged confirmation before closing the study.
I’ll test the frozen glass ensemble on held-out element combinations. This separates interpolation within familiar alloy systems from the more demanding question of transfer to new systems.
I’ll check the final glass replications and record the robustness results together, keeping them separate from the original model-selection evidence.
I’ll review the last results and publish a concise replication note. This will make grouped-validation limits and prediction-interface checks visible without presenting them as new methods.

The principal contributions and robustness checks are published. I’ll wait for the unchanged glass replications before writing the closing record, rather than infer their outcome from earlier results.
The unchanged glass model improves on both another shuffled split and held-out alloy systems. I’ll publish these checks, explicitly noting that absolute error rises when transferring to new systems.
The methods, controlled comparison, replication notes, and target-free prediction interfaces are published. I’ll leave them frozen and finish the session without further tuning.
